body_markdown:
How many wheels should a motorcycle have? Most dictionaries, including the Oxford English Dictionary, Merriam-Webster, and Cambridge, define motorcycles as having an engine and two wheels. Nonetheless, a four-wheeled vehicle, the Daimler riding carriage, or Reitwagen, is widely recognized as the first motorcycle. (It’s worth noting that the[first automobile](https://www.hagerty.com/media/magazine-features/hagerty-magazine/1886-benz-patent-motorwagen-slow-to-wake/) had three wheels, so maybe definitions can afford some flexibility.) What’s not in question, though, is that the technology came together 141 years ago and changed transportation forever.


The early days of the automobile were wild by modern standards since there were literally no standards to discuss. Around the world, inventors and tinkerers were trying various combinations of parts and techniques in attempts to create locomotion on land without the size and scale of a rail engine. The result was a means of transportation that certainly doesn’t look like today’s vehicles, but in the function-over-form world of the late 1800s it’s easy to see why.


Mercedes Benz


The Reitwagen was the creation of Gottlieb Daimler and Wilhelm Maybach, the latter of whom submitted a patent for the design on August 29, 1885. This marks the first road-going combustion engine, and though it looks like an overly elaborate toy, it’s not that far in principle from a modern motorcycle. The engine is a single vertical cylinder and displaces 264 cubic centimeters, or roughly 16 cubic inches, and made just half a horsepower. Engine speed neared 1000 rpm, though consistent spark ignition was difficult to achieve back then. A hot bulb extending to the combustion chamber via a simple tube initiated the spark. That’s right, external combustion to create internal combustion.


The engine is known as the “grandfather clock engine” and it’s easy to see why.


Mohan S


That engine was an exciting bit of tech for the era, but it wasn’t transporting anyone just by sitting on a workbench. Daimler and Maybach chose to build[a simple vehicle](https://www.mercedes-benz.com/en/art-and-culture/museum/exhibition/daimler-riding-carriage/) for the engine, as the design was not yet powerful enough to propel a larger carriage. A belt transfers power to the rear wheel, and with the engine turning 600 rpm, the vehicle could muster a blistering 6.8 mph.


That is painfully slow by today’s standards, but in the era this machine was more than proof of concept. Daimler’s son, Adolf, took the Reitwagen on a trip on November 10th, 1885, leaving Cannstatt, Germany, and traversing what could only be rudimentary roads all the way to the town of Untertürkheim. It was a journey of nearly 7.5 miles that included such excitement as the seat catching fire due to the location of the hot bulb for the ignition. Remember the external combustion part of this design? And we think managing heat in a tightly packed modern engine compartment is bad.


Oh, how far have the vehicles we use today come from the contraptions of old. It was a functional contraption, though, and set the stage for things to come. While the first automobile survived and still exists in the Mercedes-Benz museum in Germany, the Reitwagen fell victim to a fire that destroyed the Daimler plant in Cannstatt in 1903. Replicas can be found around the world, though, in case you were curious to see such a rudimentary machine in person to remember just how far vehicles have gone in the last 141 years.
